project: A bank of 48 parcel lockers in an apartment block: couriers drop, residents collect with a code that expires.

steps.title: Forty-eight doors, and a wall you can look at
steps.scene: Farida has run the parcel room out of a spiral notebook for six years. Twenty small doors, twenty medium, eight large. The notebook is the only thing that knows which of them are free.
steps.build: Load the doors and residents once at start-up from a settings object, and serve a wall that can be read and filtered by size and by free-or-holding — where free is derived from what is inside the door, never stored as a flag that can disagree with the parcels.
steps.follows: Nothing can happen until the place exists.

story.want: see every one of the 48 doors with its size and whether it is holding something
story.so: I can answer 'is there space' without walking the lobby

steps.summary: The app starts with the 48 doors and the residents loaded once, and answers a filterable wall.

doors(id, tower_id, no, size_class S|M|L, current_parcel_id nullable) — 20 S, 20 M, 8 L
residents(id, tower_id, flat, name) — loaded from seed/residents.csv
seed files: seed/doors.csv, seed/residents.csv, read once at start-up
rules: A door is `free` when current_parcel_id is null and `holding` otherwise. State is derived on read — there is no stored flag.
Seeding runs before the server accepts its first request and is idempotent: a second start-up does not duplicate rows.
Settings come from one settings object read at start-up (database path, free window hours, host, port); nothing is hard-coded.
Filters are validated: a value outside the enum is 400, not an empty list.
Filters are typed query parameters bound to enums; every response goes through a declared response model (no bare dicts).

steps.title: A courier asks for a door
steps.scene: Imran arrives with eleven parcels and a flat number written on each. He does not care which door he gets; he cares that the app answers before the lift does.
steps.build: A drop endpoint taking a size class and a flat number through a request model with real constraints, answering 201 with the door it chose — and telling a malformed body (422) apart from a flat that does not exist (400).
steps.follows: The wall is readable; this is the first thing that changes it, which is why validation has to land here.

story.want: book a parcel in by size and flat number and be given a door
story.so: I can drop eleven parcels without deciding anything myself

steps.summary: A courier books a drop by size and flat and is answered with the door that was chosen.

data: parcels(id, tower_id, flat, size_class, door_id, dropped_at, collected_at nullable, state holding|collected)
doors.current_parcel_id is set in the same transaction
rules: `size_class` must be one of S, M, L; `flat` must match a resident in this tower.
The door chosen is a free door of exactly the parcel's size class, lowest door number first.
If no door of that size is free, refuse with 409 /errors/no-door-free and list `free_sizes`.
Choosing the door and creating the parcel happen in one transaction; a failure leaves neither.
The request model uses `Field` constraints; a body that fails them is 422, a body that passes but asks for something impossible is 400 — two different types, tested separately.

steps.title: The code that dies at midnight
steps.scene: Mrs Rao is at her sister's until Sunday. The code she was given on Thursday should not still open door D22 next month.
steps.build: Issue a one-time code, store it hashed, compare it in constant time, and expire it against a free window read from an injected clock instead of the system time — so a test can move time rather than sleep through it.
steps.follows: A parcel now sits in a door. Without an expiry nothing ever comes out of it; without an injected clock the expiry can never be tested. Every time-based rule depends on this one dependency.

story.want: get a pickup code that stops working after the free window
story.so: a code read over my shoulder last week cannot open my door today

steps.summary: Every drop issues a one-time pickup code that expires, and time comes from an injected clock.

codes: as the drop answer, now with `code` and `expires_at`

data: parcels gains code_hash (never the code), code_expires_at, code_used_at nullable
rules: The code is six random digits from a cryptographic source, shown once in the drop response, and stored only as a hash.
`expires_at` = dropped_at + FREE_WINDOW_HOURS, computed from the injected clock, never from the system time inside the service.
Comparison of a presented code against the hash is constant-time.
The clock is a dependency (`Depends(get_clock)`) so a test can override it with a fixed time.
Both the database session and the clock are `Depends` dependencies, so a test overrides either without touching the route.

code_hash is present and is not the code; no column contains the plain code
the clock is fixed at T in tests

done: Codes are issued, hashed, expiring, and testable under a fixed clock.
No log line and no response contains a plain code except the drop response itself.

steps.title: Three ways to say no
steps.scene: Imran's last parcel is a 32-inch television carton and every large door is holding something. The notebook's answer was a shrug; the app has to say which size is free and why this one is not. At the keypad, a mistyped code and a code that has run out need their own answers too.
steps.build: Three refusals, each with its own code and its own status: too big for any free door, a code that never existed, a code whose window has passed — raised from a service function, never from inside the route.
steps.follows: The happy path is built. A locker wall is defined by what it refuses, and these three refusals are the first rows of its rule table.

story.want: be told which size is free when my parcel does not fit
story.so: I know whether to wait, come back, or take it away

steps.summary: Three refusals, each with its own type and status, raised from the service and mapped once.

codes: no free door of that size; `free_sizes` lists the sizes that are free
the code does not exist in this tower
the code exists but its window has passed

rules: Domain refusals are exceptions raised in the service layer (NoDoorFree, NoSuchCode, CodeExpired), never HTTP responses built inside a route.
One exception handler maps each domain exception to its status and problem type; the mapping table is the single source of truth.
`/errors/no-such-code` and `/errors/code-expired` both answer 404 so an attacker cannot tell a wrong code from an old one — but the `type` differs so the caretaker's screen can.
The exception → status mapping lives in one `exception_handler` registration; routes never build error responses.

I key the code
I am told the code does not exist
ac_api: the body has exactly type, title, status, detail and the fields the ticket names — no stack trace
done: All three refusals are produced by the service and mapped by one handler.
A test per refusal asserts status and type.
No route contains `raise HTTPException` / `ResponseStatusException` for a domain rule.

try.do: Key 000000. Then key the code from your message. (A code past its window is proven by the tests, which move the clock.)
try.see: 404 no-such-code, then 400 /errors/domain: on this ticket a right code is refused too, because opening the door is not part of this ticket. Each refusal has its own `type`. An expired code is also a 404, so a stranger cannot tell a wrong code from an old one, but its type is code-expired.

steps.title: The door opens, and the clock stops
steps.scene: Mrs Rao gets back on Sunday, keys in her code, and door D22 swings open. From that moment the wall must show D22 free for Imran's next parcel, with nobody resetting anything, and the same code must never open it again. The app also stamps how long the parcel waited: dwell time is the number the society judges the wall on.
steps.build: Accepting a valid code opens the door, frees it, and stamps dwell time on the parcel — all three in one transaction, so the wall can never show a freed door still holding a parcel.
steps.follows: The code is issued; this is the only ticket that consumes it. Until now the wall fills up and never empties.

story.want: key in my code and have the door open and free itself

The close is one session transaction: all writes or none; the test injects a failure after the first write and asserts nothing persisted.

steps.title: A notebook nobody can rewrite
steps.scene: Two months ago a parcel went missing and the notebook had been neatly tidied. Farida wants a record where a mistake is a new line, not an erased one.
steps.build: An append-only log: one row per transition — dropped, code issued, opened — written in the same transaction as the change itself, never updated and never deleted.
steps.follows: A parcel's life is now complete; this records it, and a log like this cannot be bolted on afterwards.

story.want: see every drop, code and opening in a record that cannot be edited
story.so: when a parcel is disputed there is one account of what happened

steps.summary: Every transition is written to an append-only log in the same transaction, and can be read back per parcel.
data: events(id, tower_id, parcel_id, kind dropped|code_issued|opened|swept|rehomed|charged|notified, at, data json) — insert only
no UPDATE or DELETE is ever issued against events; enforce it (a database rule/trigger, or a repository with no update method and a test that proves it)
rules: An event is written inside the same transaction as the state change it records; a rolled-back drop leaves no `dropped` event.
Events carry ids and facts, never the plain code or the resident's name.
The parcel's `events` are returned in `at` order and are the only history the UI shows.
Event rows are inserted with a plain INSERT in the same session transaction as the change; the events model has no update path.

a drop that fails after the insert

done: Every transition writes an event in-transaction.
Immutability is enforced and tested, not assumed.
GET /parcels/{id} returns the ordered events.

steps.title: One file becomes an app
steps.scene: Imran's dispatcher asks for the API docs so their own system can book drops. What exists is one module and an error format that changes shape depending on which line raised it.
steps.build: Routers for doors, drops, pickups and parcels; one exception handler giving every refusal the same shape; tags, summaries and documented error responses, so /docs is something a courier's developer could work from.
steps.follows: The rules so far have piled into one file. This is where it stops being a script, and the error shape is settled here.

story.want: read one set of API docs where every refusal has the same shape
story.so: our system can book drops without guessing what an error means

steps.summary: The app is split into modules with one error shape and API docs another team can build against.

codes: renders every endpoint with its summary, tags (doors, drops, pickups, parcels) and each documented error response
the machine-readable spec; every 4xx in the codes tables appears on the endpoint that can return it

rules: Routers: doors, drops, pickups, parcels — each in its own module under `lockerline/routers/`; the service and rules modules hold no FastAPI imports.
Exactly one exception handler produces every error body, including validation errors and unexpected exceptions (500 with a generic detail, no stack trace).
Every endpoint declares its error responses in the spec with an example body.
`APIRouter` per resource, mounted from one `app.py`; services and rules import nothing from FastAPI.

steps.title: The rule table, and then the rule changes
steps.scene: The society votes to halve the free window: forty-eight hours becomes twenty-four. Farida's real question is whether anything else moved when it did.
steps.build: A parametrised table of every refusal the wall can give, driven through the test client with the clock overridden — then change the window to 24 hours and watch exactly one row of the table move.
steps.follows: The refusals exist and time can be moved. Only now can a rule be changed with evidence instead of hope.

story.want: change the free window from 48 hours to 24 and see exactly which rules moved
story.so: a policy change does not quietly break a rule nobody was thinking about

steps.summary: A parametrised rule table covers every refusal, and the free window can change without breaking anything else.
data: no new tables; FREE_WINDOW_HOURS is read from settings at start-up
rules: The rule table is one parametrised test with one row per case: fits / right size gone (refused) / nothing fits / code used / code expired / inside the window / past the window. Each row names given, action, expected status and type.
Rows come from a CSV or a list passed to `pytest.mark.parametrize`; the clock is overridden with `dependency_overrides`.
Changing FREE_WINDOW_HOURS from 48 to 24 changes the outcome of exactly the expiry rows and no others; the table proves it.
The table is one `@pytest.mark.parametrize` over `TestClient` with `dependency_overrides` for the clock; the rule change is a settings override in the same test module.

ac_api: every refusal type the wall can give so far appears in at least one row, and every row passes
only the rows tagged `window` change outcome
done: The table exists, is parametrised, and covers all six refusal/happy rows.
A second run with the window at 24 shows the documented rows moving and no others.
GET /settings exists and the UI reads it.

steps.title: It runs on a machine that isn't yours
steps.scene: Vikram has an old mini-PC in the society office. He wants the parcel room running on it, and he is not going to install Python.
steps.build: A Dockerfile for the app, an image built and run with a mapped port, and HOST=0.0.0.0 so it answers from outside the container.
steps.follows: The app is finished and tested; this is the first day it leaves your laptop.

story.want: run the parcel room from a single image on the office machine
story.so: I do not have to install a development environment to use it

steps.summary: The app builds into an image and runs in a container, answering on a mapped port from outside.

codes: the process is up and can reach its database

rules: Dockerfile: `python:3.12-slim`, dependencies installed from a lock file, `HOST=0.0.0.0`, `PORT=8080`, `CMD uvicorn lockerline.app:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080`.
`docker build -t lockerline .` and `docker run -p 8080:8080 lockerline` are the only two commands needed; the README shows them.
The container answers GET on the health path from the host.

steps.title: It survives being switched off
steps.scene: Vikram unplugs the mini-PC to vacuum behind it. Every parcel in the wall disappears.
steps.build: A volume that keeps the data, configuration through an env-file rather than baked into the image, a .dockerignore, logs to stdout — and the README that walks one parcel from drop to collection.
steps.follows: The image ran once. This is what turns it into something Vikram can be handed.

story.want: restart or unplug the machine without losing the parcels
story.so: a power cut is an inconvenience rather than an incident

steps.summary: Data survives `docker rm`, configuration comes from an env-file, logs go to stdout, and the README hands it over.
data: the SQLite file lives on a named volume mounted at /data; DATABASE_URL=sqlite:////data/lockerline.db
.dockerignore excludes tests, .git, local databases and virtualenvs / build output
rules: Every setting (database path, FREE_WINDOW_HOURS, HOST, PORT) is read from environment variables via `--env-file`; nothing is baked into the image.
All logs go to stdout/stderr, one line per event; no log file inside the container.
README: how to build, run with a volume and env-file, and a walkthrough of one parcel from drop to collection with the exact curl calls.
Settings are read by pydantic-settings from the environment; the env-file is the only configuration input.
